summary: Satellites have tracked active fires for more than two decades, but the record is split across instruments whose counts cannot be compared directly. VIIRS has finer pixels than MODIS, so it reports several times more hotspots for the same fires; over the contiguous United States, the raw count jumps 6.6-fold in 2012, the year the instrument changes. A fire manager reading that record cannot tell whether this month is truly unusual or the sensor is simply more sensitive. Burn Calendar harmonizes NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS Aqua, VIIRS S-NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20 into a single consistent record from 2003 to the present. Using the years when the instruments overlap, we derive a conversion for each region and calendar month and place every value on a common scale. In the web application, a user draws any area and sees its year-by-month burn calendar, its burning season, its worst years, and how the current month compares with the same days in earlier years; all results can be downloaded as CSV. The need is pressing: S-NPP stopped producing fire data on 2 November 2026, and MODIS is nearing the end of its mission. We validate the conversion on years withheld from fitting, attach an uncertainty range to every converted value, and state plainly where the method is weak.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Burn Calendar is a static web application. For any area inside four regions (the contiguous United States, Taiwan, Myanmar with Thailand and Laos, and Argentina) it answers three questions:

  • Is this month worse than usual?
  • Which months are the burning season, and which years were the worst?
  • Where does each number come from, and how certain is it?

The user never needs to know which satellite produced a number. Values converted from another instrument are marked, and the original value is one click away.

Website: https://nasa.vicvic88.net

Code: https://github.com/viccode88/nasa-space-apps-2026

HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

  1. Filter. We keep presumed vegetation fires (FIRMS type 0) with MODIS confidence of 30 or more, or VIIRS confidence nominal or high. For MODIS we use Aqua only, because Aqua and the VIIRS satellites pass at about the same local time. Terra passes in the morning.
  2. Grid. Hotspots are assigned to 0.1 degree cells and UTC days. We report two metrics: active cell-days (a cell with at least one hotspot on a day) and equivalent hotspots. Cell-days are less sensitive to pixel size: the raw gap between the instruments is 3.6 times for cell-days and 6.6 times for hotspots.
  3. Learn the conversion. In the years when two instruments observed the same places, the conversion coefficient is the ratio of their totals. We compute one coefficient per subregion and calendar month, because the ratio changes with fire type and season. For MODIS Aqua cell-days it ranges from 2.7 to 9.2. Aqua is trained on 2012-2021 only, before its orbit began to drift. NOAA-20 is trained on 2018-2025.
  4. Build one series. 2003-01 to 2012-01 is MODIS Aqua multiplied by its coefficient. 2012-02 to 2026-10 is VIIRS S-NPP as observed. From 2026-11 it is VIIRS NOAA-20 multiplied by its coefficient. Every value is on the VIIRS S-NPP scale.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

Leave-one-year-out cross-validation: for each year, the coefficients are computed without that year and used to predict it.

  • MODIS Aqua to VIIRS S-NPP: bias within 1.1% and monthly error of 9% to 21% in the four large subregions. Our targets were 10% and 30%.
  • VIIRS NOAA-20 to VIIRS S-NPP: bias within 0.2% and monthly error of 3% to 10%.
  • The contiguous United States averaged 29,921 active cell-days per year in 2003-2011 before harmonization and 116,615 after, against 108,250 in 2013-2025. The jump of 2012 is gone.

We also report what does not work. The ranking of years by total fire activity misses our target (rank correlation of 0.8) for cell-days in the western United States (0.46) and in Myanmar, Thailand and Laos (0.79). Taiwan has too few fires to fit a seasonal conversion, so its values before 2012 carry a very wide range. Every converted value is shown with the 10% to 90% range from cross-validation, and the methods page lists eleven limitations.

THE WEB APPLICATION

  • Select an area: draw a rectangle on the map, type its edges, or pick a region, and choose the first and last month. An area outside the covered regions gets a "not covered" message, never a count of zero, and the page says how much of a rectangle is sea or another country.
  • Headline: the current month so far, compared with the median of the same days in earlier years, with its range and its rank. For the contiguous United States on 13 November 2026: 4,924 active cell-days, close to the median of 4,821, 11th highest of 24 years.
  • Burn calendar: one row per year and one column per month, from 2003 to today, with the number in every cell. Converted months are hatched, so color is never the only signal. Each month shows its value, range, sensor, raw value, coefficient and rank.
  • Anomaly view: the difference from the median of each calendar month, on a blue-to-orange scale.
  • Key facts and charts: the burning season, the highest year, annual totals, the spread of each calendar month, and an outlook for the next three months taken from the record. The outlook is labelled as history, not a forecast.
  • CSV download of the calendar and of the individual hotspots in the selected area. Each file starts with lines that cite FIRMS and describe the harmonization.
  • The selection is kept in the page address, so a view can be shared as a link.
  • A methods page with the validation figures and tables for every region.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Early warning and emergency responders can see within seconds whether current fire activity is unusual for the time of year. Land managers can identify burning seasons and compare years across the whole record. Scientists can inspect the coefficients, the uncertainty and the original detections, and rebuild every data file with one command.

S-NPP stopped producing fire data on 2 November 2026 and MODIS is near the end of its mission. Without harmonization, more than twenty years of fire history cannot be compared with any future observation. Burn Calendar keeps that history usable.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • We count active cell-days, not only hotspots. A large fire that fills a cell counts once for either instrument, which removes almost half of the gap between them before any conversion.
  • The current month is compared with the same days of earlier years, not with full months, so an unfinished month is never read as a quiet one.
  • Converted values are hatched and carry a range. The page separates what was observed from what was estimated.
  • Sensor outages are detected from the fire record itself: a sensor's count collapsing on different continents on the same day points to the sensor, not the weather. We found 54 such days for S-NPP and removed them from training.
  • "No fire" and "no data" are kept apart. A list of covered cells lets the page say "not covered" over another country or the sea.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

  • Orbit drift: Aqua's overpass time has drifted since about 2022, so those years are not used to learn its conversion.
  • Fixed heat sources: recent near-real-time data has no type field, so industrial sources are removed with a mask. Our first mask removed up to 35% of real fires in Taiwan. We compared eight designs on held-out years and chose one that changes totals by less than 0.5%.
  • Regions with different fire regimes, to test the method: summer forest fires in the western United States, prescribed and agricultural burning in the east, spring burning in mainland Southeast Asia, whose smoke reaches Taiwan, a Southern Hemisphere season in Argentina, and Taiwan as a low-fire case that shows the limits.
  • Accessibility: color scales chosen for color-vision deficiency (cividis and blue-to-orange, no red-green contrast), numbers in every cell, and keyboard access to every month.
  • Reliability: the site has no server and calls no external API at run time, apart from map tiles.
  • Honesty about limits: results that miss our targets are reported next to those that meet them.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

  • Data pipeline: Python, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, SciPy, Shapely, Matplotlib.
  • Web application: TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet, DuckDB-WASM, Apache ECharts.
  • Data format: Apache Parquet, queried in the browser.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Workers, serving static files.
  • About 40 million FIRMS detections were processed. The application serves 18.6 million hotspots and 6.4 million active cell-days.

USE OF SI

The data pipeline, the web application and first drafts of the documentation were written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), following the team's specification. All figures are plotted from data; none are SI-generated images.

WHAT COMES NEXT

  • Extend coverage from four regions to the globe.
  • Add NOAA-21 as a second continuing instrument.
  • Replace the derived list of outage days with the official FIRMS record.
  • Test other conversions where the ratio method ranks years poorly.

FIRMS country files: MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS S-NPP 375 m and VIIRS NOAA-20 375 m active fire data
